# Global agent rules

These apply in every repo. A repo's own AGENTS.md wins where it's more specific.

## Git

Git history belongs to the user. Inspect freely, change the working tree as the task needs, and leave committing, pushing, and branch changes to them. Finish with the commit-preparation summary from the `git-workflow` skill.

## Done means proven

Before reporting a task complete, run the checks the repo defines (tests, typecheck, lint) and show the result. For anything with behavior, prove it against the real artifact, using `verify`. Label every claim as checked, inferred, or guessed.

## Code

Ponytail is on for code size and reuse. Beyond it:

- When adding a dependency, change only that package, keep lockfile changes to what it needs, and check its maintenance and install scripts.
- Leave unrelated dependencies at their current versions.

## Prose

Anything the user will read goes through `unslop`. Anything sent or published under their name goes through `my-voice`. No em dashes in either.

## Asking

Look up facts yourself. Ask only for decisions that are the user's to make: product calls, scope, anything irreversible or customer-facing.

---
name: client-estimate
description: Scope and price client work. Use when estimating a client project, pricing a modernization or rewrite of a legacy codebase, sizing a phased engagement, or drafting a proposal or quote.
---

# Client estimate

Produce an estimate a client can trust and that you can deliver without eating the overrun. An honest wide range beats an optimistic narrow one. Every number traces back to something found in the code or stated by the client.

## 1. Pin the ask

Write down what the client actually needs, in their words, and what decision the estimate feeds: approve a budget, choose between paths, compare vendors. Note who approves the spend and any budget signal they've given.

Done when you can state the ask in two sentences the client would agree with.

## 2. Find out what's really there

If you have the code, run `/ponytail-audit` for the ranked findings, then add the inventory an estimate needs, with counts:

- Stacks and versions, including anything end-of-life.
- Size by surface: pages, routes, components, endpoints, stored procedures, jobs, integrations.
- Data: databases, schemas, who else reads them.
- Tenancy and customization: per-client branches, flags, hardcoded carve-outs.
- Deploy, CI, and source control.
- Security findings, flagged as must-fix regardless of what the client buys.

If you don't have access yet, say so up front, price as an "in the dark" range, and say what access would narrow it. Never present an in-the-dark number as firm.

## 3. Split into phases that each deliver something

Break the work into phases the client could stop after and still have something useful. Put security fixes and quick wins first, since those are often the only piece that gets approved. Keep independent pieces as separate line items so the client can approve one now.

For each architectural fork, like wrap versus decompose, or rewrite versus incremental, present both paths with their own ranges and let the client choose. Don't silently price one.

## 4. Price each phase

Price from the inventory. Use a per-unit rate where units are countable, like days per component by complexity tier. Show the unit, the count, and the rate so the client can follow the math. Then add what typing-time estimates miss:

- rediscovering business logic that lives only in code or stored procedures
- parallel running or cutover for live systems
- verification across every tenant or integration
- client-side delays: access, approvals, environments

Ask the hard question about each phase: is familiarity with the stack being counted as lower cost? Comfort isn't speed. Then reconcile the phases against any number already sent. If they don't fit, say so plainly, with the gap.

## 5. Deliver

- **Internal breakdown.** Inventory, per-phase math, assumptions, risks, and where the range could move. For the user, not the client.
- **Client version.** Problem in their terms, phases with what each delivers, ranges, assumptions, what's excluded, and what would narrow the range. Written through `my-voice`.

Name the riskiest assumption in the estimate in one line at the end.

---
name: comments
description: Code comment rules for writing or reviewing source comments. Default to none, keep the rare one to a single line about a why the code can't show, and treat a long comment as a sign the code needs reshaping.
---

# Comments

Default to no comments. Names, types, and structure carry the meaning.

## A comment earns its place when deleting it invites a breaking "cleanup"

Write one line that names a constraint the code can't show:

- an external system's behavior: `// Must stay sequential: the upstream API rejects concurrent writes.`
- a browser or library quirk: `// Safari needs this focus call before the picker opens.`
- an ordering invariant: `// Check the signature before normalizing; it covers the raw payload.`
- the proven fact behind an unavoidable cast or suppression: `// Zod parsed this above; the SDK types don't expose the shape.`
- a deliberate shortcut, in ponytail's format, so `/ponytail-debt` can list it: `// shortcut: in-memory cache, move to Redis when we run more than one process.`

Public API doc comments and license headers stay too.

## When a comment wants to grow

Reshape the code instead:

- the name doesn't say what it does: rename it
- a block needs a paragraph to justify itself: extract a named function
- comments narrate steps: make each step a named call
- a magic value needs explaining: give it a named constant

## What goes elsewhere

History, ticket numbers, who asked for it, and "added for the billing flow" belong in the commit message. A TODO for work this task needs means doing the work now. Deferred work goes in a `shortcut:` comment or the issue list.

## Reviewing

Delete comments that narrate what the code plainly does. When a comment is propping up a confusing name or structure, recommend the code change. Keep comments that state a real constraint.

---
name: correct
description: Retro on a session or a repeated correction. Turns mistakes agents keep making into checks that make them impossible.
disable-model-invocation: true
argument-hint: "[session or mistake to look at]"
---

# Correct

Assume the next contributor is an agent that sees only the files it opened, copies the nearest example, and takes the shortest path that compiles. Change the repo so that path is the right one.

## 1. Collect the mistakes

Read the session the user names (the current one by default), plus recent reverts, review comments, and the corrections the user gave. Group them into classes. A class counts once it has happened twice, or once if it was expensive.

Also look for:

- **Navigation.** The agent took a long time to find something. A pointer in AGENTS.md or `docs/agents/` would fix it.
- **Missing access.** It needed information it couldn't get: dev server logs, a dashboard, a schema.
- **Dead weight.** Instructions in AGENTS.md or skills that changed nothing, or that a tool already enforces.

## 2. Fix each class at the highest level that works

1. **Architecture.** Give each piece of state one owner and each task one supported way. Hide internals so the wrong import fails. Delete the old way the agent keeps copying.
2. **Types.** Make the bad state impossible to write.
3. **Lint.** A custom lint rule whose error message names the fix, like "use `<Flex>` from `ui/layout` instead of a raw flex `div`". If the pattern is already common, fail only when a change adds more.
4. **Test.** One that fails on the real past mistake.
5. **Docs.** Last, and only for judgment calls nothing can check.

## 3. Prove it

For each new check, reproduce the past mistake and show the check fails on it. A check that has never been red hasn't been proven.

## 4. Report

For each class: the evidence, the level you chose, and why a higher level didn't work. Then the files changed and the commit-preparation summary from `git-workflow`. When a rule already existed in docs and the mistake still happened, nothing enforced it, so move it up a level.

---
name: diagnose
description: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when asked to debug or diagnose, or when something is broken, throwing, failing, flaky, or slow and the cause isn't obvious.
---

# Diagnose

Find the root cause with evidence, then fix it once in the shared code. Phases run in order. Skip one only with a stated reason.

Redact secrets in everything you show. Build commands against env vars so credentials stay out of the transcript.

## 1. Build a red loop

This is the whole skill. Get one command that goes **red** on this exact bug. Then bisection, hypotheses, and instrumentation all just consume it. Without one, reading code produces theories, not answers.

Try these roughly in order:

1. A failing Vitest test at whatever seam reaches the bug.
2. A curl or script against the running dev server.
3. A CLI or script call with a fixture input, diffed against known-good output.
4. A Playwright script that drives the UI and asserts on DOM, console, or network.
5. A captured request or event replayed through the code path in isolation.
6. A throwaway harness that boots the smallest slice of the system with one function call.
7. A loop over many random inputs, for "sometimes wrong" bugs.
8. A `git bisect run` script, when it worked at a known earlier state.
9. A differential run: same input through old and new versions, diffed.

Then make it **tight**: seconds not minutes, same verdict every run, asserting the user's exact symptom rather than "didn't crash". For flaky bugs, raise the reproduction rate (loop it, add load, narrow timing) until it's high enough to work against.

Done when you have shown one command, its invocation, and its red output. If you can't build one, stop and say what you tried. Ask for access to the failing environment, a captured artifact (HAR, log dump, recording), or permission to add temporary instrumentation. Don't move on to theories without a loop.

## 2. Reproduce and minimize

Confirm the loop shows the failure the user described, not a nearby one. Then cut inputs, data, config, and steps one at a time, rerunning after each cut. Done when every remaining piece is load-bearing: removing any one turns the loop green.

## 3. Hypothesize

Write 3 to 5 ranked hypotheses before testing any. Each makes a falsifiable prediction: "If X is the cause, changing Y makes it disappear." A hypothesis without a prediction is a vibe, so sharpen it or drop it. Show the ranked list to the user, who often knows something that reorders it, then continue with your ranking without waiting.

## 4. Instrument

Each probe tests one prediction and changes one variable. Prefer a debugger or REPL, then targeted logs at the boundaries that separate hypotheses. Tag every debug log with a unique prefix like `[DEBUG-a4f2]` so cleanup is one grep. For performance, measure a baseline first (timing harness, profiler, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`), then bisect against it.

## 5. Fix at the root

Ask why until you reach the cause, and fix it there. A null check that silences the crash is a symptom guard, not a fix. Before editing, grep every caller of the function you're changing.

Turn the minimized repro into a regression test at a seam that exercises the real bug pattern. Watch it fail, apply the fix, watch it pass, then rerun the original phase 1 loop. If no seam can catch the bug honestly, say so. That's an architecture finding worth reporting.

If two fixes built on the same assumption have both failed, stop fixing. Question the assumption itself.

## 6. Clean up

- [ ] The original loop is green.
- [ ] The regression test passes, or the missing seam is reported.
- [ ] `grep` for the debug prefix returns nothing.
- [ ] Throwaway harnesses are deleted.
- [ ] The confirmed hypothesis goes in the suggested commit message, so the next person debugging learns it.

---
name: git-workflow
description: Apply the user's Git safety and commit-preparation preferences when working in repositories. Never commit, push, merge, rebase, cherry-pick, or discard user changes unless explicitly instructed. Inspect and modify the working tree as needed, then identify the files or specific hunks that should be committed and propose Conventional Commit messages.
---

# Git workflow

Treat Git history and the user's existing changes as human-owned.

The agent may inspect the repository and modify the working tree, but must never create or publish Git history on its own.

## Never commit or publish

Never run or perform:

- `git commit`
- `git push`
- `git merge`
- `git rebase`
- `git cherry-pick`

Do not use aliases, scripts, IDE integrations, or other mechanisms that perform these operations indirectly.

Do not create commits merely because the requested implementation is complete.

The user decides when and how changes become history.

## Never discard user work

Do not discard, overwrite, or reset changes that the user has made unless explicitly instructed.

Never use destructive operations such as:

- `git reset --hard`
- `git restore` on user-modified files
- `git checkout` to overwrite changes
- deleting untracked files
- force-updating branches

Before modifying files, inspect the working tree when necessary to distinguish existing user changes from work introduced during the current task.

Preserve unrelated changes.

## Do not silently alter history or branch state

Do not:

- Rewrite commit history.
- Force-push.
- Delete branches.
- Change remotes.
- Change Git configuration globally.
- Rebase or reorder commits.
- Amend existing commits.

Branch creation or switching is also a state-changing Git operation. Do not do it unless explicitly requested or clearly necessary for the task.

When a task can be completed without changing branches, leave the current branch alone.

## Staging

Do not stage changes merely because they are ready to commit.

Leave the index alone unless the user explicitly asks for staging or a Git operation that requires it.

When the work is complete, tell the user exactly what should be staged.

Be precise about hunks when a file contains unrelated changes.

For example:

```text
Stage:
- src/client.ts — lines 42-67, the timeout handling change
- src/client.test.ts — the new timeout test

Do not stage:
- src/client.ts — the unrelated formatting changes already present
```

Use `git diff`, `git diff --cached`, and related inspection commands to understand the working tree and identify the appropriate changes.

## Preserve unrelated work

A repository may already contain changes unrelated to the current task.

Do not:

- Reformat unrelated files.
- Clean up unrelated code.
- Rename unrelated identifiers.
- Modify unrelated tests.
- Include unrelated changes in the proposed commit.

If an existing change makes the requested work ambiguous, inspect the diff and work around it rather than reverting it.

## Commit preparation

When implementation is complete, provide a concise commit-ready summary.

Identify:

1. The files that belong in the commit.
2. Specific hunks when only part of a file should be included.
3. Any files that should explicitly remain unstaged.
4. One or more suggested commit messages.

Do not stage or commit them yourself.

## Conventional Commits

Suggest commit messages following Conventional Commits:

```text
<type>(<scope>): <description>
```

Use a type that accurately describes the change, such as:

- `feat`
- `fix`
- `refactor`
- `perf`
- `test`
- `docs`
- `build`
- `ci`
- `chore`

Use a scope when the repository has a natural component, package, feature, or domain for it.

Keep the subject concise and imperative.

Prefer:

```text
fix(environmental): handle EDR timeout responses
```

over:

```text
fix: fixed some issues with EDR API calls
```

Do not invent a scope if the repository does not use meaningful scopes.

Do not force a `BREAKING CHANGE` unless the change actually breaks the public contract.

## Split logical changes

When the working tree contains multiple logically independent changes, recommend separate commits rather than one large commit.

For example:

```text
Suggested commits:

1. fix(environmental): handle EDR timeout responses
   - src/edr/client.ts
   - src/edr/errors.ts

2. test(environmental): cover EDR timeout handling
   - src/edr/client.test.ts
```

Keep the suggested history meaningful and reviewable.

Do not split changes artificially just to create more commits.

## Commit message should describe the result

Describe what changed, not the process used to get there.

Prefer:

```text
feat(auth): support SSO session refresh
```

over:

```text
feat(auth): refactor authentication code and fix tests
```

unless the refactor itself is the meaningful result.

Avoid vague subjects such as:

```text
fix bugs
updates
misc changes
cleanup
work on API
```

## Git inspection is encouraged

Read-only Git operations are encouraged when they help understand the task:

- `git status`
- `git diff`
- `git diff --check`
- `git log`
- `git show`
- `git blame`
- inspecting branches and remotes
- inspecting tracked and untracked files

Use repository history when it provides useful context for understanding an implementation or preserving established conventions.

Do not inspect excessive history without a reason.

## Final response

When the work is complete, report the implementation result and then provide the Git preparation section.

Use a format like:

```text
### Commit preparation

Stage:
- src/foo.ts — hunks implementing X
- src/foo.test.ts — tests covering Y

Leave unstaged:
- src/foo.ts — pre-existing changes unrelated to this task

Suggested commit:
fix(foo): handle invalid response payloads
```

When there are multiple logical commits:

```text
### Commit preparation

1. Stage:
   - src/foo.ts — ...
   - src/foo.test.ts — ...

   Suggested commit:
   fix(foo): handle invalid response payloads

2. Stage:
   - src/bar.ts — ...

   Suggested commit:
   refactor(bar): simplify response handling
```

Do not provide a fake commit hash.

Do not imply that anything was committed or pushed.

## Final safety check

Before finishing, verify:

- No commit was created.
- Nothing was pushed.
- No existing commit was rewritten.
- No user changes were discarded.
- Unrelated changes remain untouched.
- The recommended files and hunks are clearly identified.
- Suggested commit messages follow Conventional Commits.

---
name: grill
description: Interview the user in rounds to stress-test a plan, design, or decision until nothing is left assumed. Use when asked to grill, poke holes in, pressure-test, or sanity-check a plan before building.
---

# Grill

Map the plan as a decision tree: each decision branches into the ones that depend on it. Work the tree in rounds until every branch is settled.

## Rounds

The **frontier** is every open decision whose prerequisites are already settled. Ask the whole frontier in one round. A question that depends on another question in the same round waits for a later one.

Format each question like this, and word it so "yes" accepts your recommendation:

```
**Q1. <short title>**
<the question, with the options if there are several>

Recommended: <your answer and the one-line reason>
```

After the user answers, recompute the frontier and ask the next round.

## Facts are your job, decisions are theirs

Never ask the user something you could look up: what the code does, what a library supports, what the schema allows. Look it up, or send a subagent while you ask the rest of the frontier. Only the questions downstream of that lookup wait. Put the product, scope, and preference calls to the user, and push back when an answer seems wrong for their own stated goals.

## Done

The session is done when the frontier is empty and nothing is silently assumed. Summarize the settled decisions as a short list. Then confirm the user agrees before acting on any of it. If they want it captured, hand off to `spec`.

---
name: handoff
description: Compact this session into a handoff document a fresh agent can pick up from.
disable-model-invocation: true
argument-hint: "[what the next session is for]"
---

# Handoff

Write a handoff file to `$TMPDIR` (or `/tmp`), never the repo. If the user said what the next session is for, tailor it to that.

Include:

- **Goal.** What we're trying to get done, in one or two sentences.
- **State.** What's finished, what's in progress, and what's verified versus only claimed.
- **Decisions.** What was settled and the reason for each, so the next agent doesn't reopen them.
- **Next step.** The single next action, specific enough to start on.
- **Watch out for.** Dead ends already tried, gotchas, anything fragile.
- **Files.** Paths to the spec, the changed files, and any scripts or repro commands.
- **Skills.** Which skills the next agent should load.

Point at specs, diffs, and docs by path instead of copying them. Redact keys, passwords, and personal data. Reply with the file path and the line to paste into the new session.

---
name: my-voice
description: Write as the user for anything they'll send or publish under their name. Use when drafting emails, client messages, proposals, posts, site copy, announcements, or resume content.
---

# My voice

Write as the user, in first person, so they can send it with light edits or none. Apply `unslop` too. These rules win where they're more specific.

## How the user writes

- Short. A client email is two to four short paragraphs, often a few sentences each.
- Direct, friendly, and appreciative without gushing. State the point, then make the next step easy.
- Conversational openers that drop the subject: "Wanted to check in...", "Know things get busy...", "Just circling back on...". A comma can join a quick aside: "Also wanted to flag, I still don't have the access we talked about."
- Low pressure. "No rush" and "happy to jump on a call if that's easier" come naturally. Never guilt-trip or manufacture urgency.
- Honest about uncertainty. Give a range and say why it's wide rather than projecting false precision.
- Plain words. No corporate phrasing like "per my last email", "circle back to align", or "I hope this email finds you well".
- No em dashes or en dashes anywhere.

## Email shape

```
Hi <first name>,

<the point, one to three sentences>

<one more practical item if there is one>

<the easy next step, often a call offer>

Thanks,
<user's first name>
```

"Talk soon," fits the warmer version. Reply in the existing thread for a follow-up, and keep its subject line.

## Variants

For anything that matters, give two versions labeled by intent, usually **Direct** and **Warmer**. They differ in tone and framing, not just word swaps. The warmer one adds a line of personal context or reassurance. Give a one-line note on when each fits.

## Proposals and longer copy

Lead with the client's problem in their own terms. Then what the work will cover, phase by phase, what each phase delivers, the price range, and the assumptions behind it. Keep the tone confident and specific: no hedging language, and no inflated claims either. Short sections, plain headings, numbers in the open.

## Before handing it over

- [ ] No em dashes, en dashes, or mid-sentence colons.
- [ ] Every sentence sounds like something the user would say out loud to the recipient.
- [ ] Facts, names, numbers, and dates are only ones the user gave or the thread contains. Mark anything you filled in as `[confirm]`.

---
name: prototype
description: Build throwaway code that answers one design question. Use when asked to prototype, mock up, try a few layouts, or check whether a state model or flow feels right before building it for real.
---

# Prototype

A prototype is throwaway code that answers a question. Write the question down first, in one line, at the top of the prototype. The question decides the shape.

## Pick the branch

- **"What should this look like?"** Build UI variants.
- **"Does this logic or state model hold up?"** Build a logic demo.

If the user isn't around to ask, pick the branch that matches where the code lives (a page or component means UI, a module means logic) and state the assumption at the top.

## UI variants

- Default to 3 variants, never more than 5. They must differ in structure: layout, information hierarchy, the primary action. Three card grids in different colors isn't a prototype.
- Mount them on the real page that would host the feature, with real data, layout, and density. Switch between them with a `?variant=a|b|c` search param, validated in the route's search schema, and a small floating bar to flip between them. Make a throwaway route only when nothing existing could host it, and put `prototype` in its path.
- Use the project's real components and theme tokens, so the comparison is honest.

## Logic demo

One self-contained HTML file the user can open directly. Free-play buttons fire each event, plus a few guided walkthroughs of the cases that are hard to reason about on paper. After every action, render the full current state, so the user sees exactly what changed.

## Rules for both

- Clearly throwaway. Keep it near the code it's for, named so nobody mistakes it for production.
- One command or one file to run.
- State in memory. If persistence is the question, use a scratch database named as a prototype.
- No tests, no polish, no abstractions. Error handling only where it keeps the thing running.

## When it's answered

Write down the verdict and the question it settled, in the spec or the conversation. Fold the winning decision into real code separately. Delete the prototype, or leave it on a local branch the user can find, and say which you did.

---
name: react
description: React conventions for writing, changing, or reviewing components and hooks. Covers when an Effect is allowed, derived state, memoization, state ownership with TanStack Query and Zustand, composable component APIs, and accessibility.
---

# React

Follow React's rendering model. Project patterns, the framework's data loading, and local AGENTS.md win over this file.

## Effects are for external systems only

An Effect synchronizes React with something outside React: the DOM, a browser API, a timer, a subscription, a socket, an imperative widget. Before writing one, name that system. If you can't, the code belongs somewhere else:

| The Effect would... | Put it here instead |
|---|---|
| compute a value from props or state | a `const` during render |
| react to a click, submit, or other user action | the event handler |
| set state that sets more state | one event handler that updates everything together |
| fetch server data | the route loader or TanStack Query |
| run once on app start | module scope or the app entry |
| reset state when a prop changes | a `key` on the component |

Every Effect returns a cleanup that undoes its setup, survives Strict Mode's double run, and lists every dependency. When the dependency list is inconvenient, restructure: move the object inside the Effect, hoist stable logic out of the component, or split the Effect. The Hooks lint rule stays on.

## State

- Store the smallest state that captures intent and derive the rest. Two pieces of state that can disagree are one piece of state.
- Keep state local until two distant parts of the tree need it, then use the project's store (Zustand) over threading props through components that don't use them.
- Server data lives in TanStack Query or the route loader, never in `useState` plus `useEffect`.
- Context carries slow-changing shared dependencies (theme, session, a compound component's internals), not fast-changing values.
- Refs hold values that must persist without causing a render. Anything that affects output is state.

## Memoization needs a reason

Add `useMemo`, `useCallback`, or `memo` only for a measured expensive computation or an identity that a memoized consumer depends on. Check the dependencies are themselves stable, or the memo recomputes every render. Everything else renders plainly. If the project runs the React Compiler, add no manual memoization at all.

## Component APIs

- Type props with a named `Props` type on the parameter. Use plain functions, not `React.FC`. Type `children` only on components that render it.
- Build compound components (`<Card>`, `<Card.Header>`, `<Card.Body>`) over one component with a pile of boolean flags. Export the composable parts plus a preassembled default for the common case.
- Follow the project's primitive layer (Base UI and shadcn) for interactive widgets. Those primitives already own focus, keyboard handling, and ARIA.
- Use stable, data-derived keys. An index is a key only for a list that never reorders.

## Accessibility

Accessibility is correctness. Use the semantic element: `<button>` for actions, `<a>` for navigation, `<label>` bound to every input. Every icon-only control gets an accessible name. Every interaction works from the keyboard, overlays close on Escape and return focus, and errors are tied to their field with `aria-describedby`. Reach for ARIA only where no native element expresses the behavior.

---
name: spec-review
description: Check a diff against the spec it was built from. Reports what's missing, what wasn't asked for, and what looks implemented but wrong. Code quality review is ponytail-review's job.
disable-model-invocation: true
argument-hint: "[spec path] [base ref]"
---

# Spec review

Answer one question: does this change do what the spec asked? Bugs, security, and style belong to `/ponytail-review`. Run both when you want a full review. Keep them separate so a clean pass on one axis can't hide a failure on the other.

## 1. Pin the diff

Use the base the user names. Otherwise use the merge-base with `main`, plus uncommitted and untracked changes, since the user doesn't commit until review is done. Confirm the ref resolves and the diff isn't empty before going further.

## 2. Find the spec

In order:

1. A path the user passed.
2. A file in `docs/specs/` or `docs/architecture/` matching the branch or feature name.
3. The implementation brief earlier in this conversation.
4. Ask. If there isn't one, say so and stop.

## 3. Check every requirement

Go through the spec line by line. For each requirement, find the code that satisfies it, or note it as missing. Then go through the diff hunk by hunk and find the requirement each hunk serves.

Done when every spec requirement and every hunk is accounted for.

## 4. Report

Quote the spec line for each finding, and give the `file:line` it points at.

- **Missing or partial.** Asked for and absent or incomplete.
- **Wrong.** Looks implemented but behaves differently than the spec says. Show the case that differs.
- **Not asked for.** Behavior in the diff with no requirement behind it. Some of it is fine scope a change naturally needs. Say which.
- **Spec gaps.** Decisions the code had to make that the spec never covered. These go back to the user, not to the code.

End with one line: the count per group and the worst finding. Change no code.

---
name: spec
description: Turn the current conversation into a spec file and an implementation brief another agent can build from. Use when asked to write a spec, write up the plan, or write a prompt or brief for a coding agent.
argument-hint: "[feature name]"
---

# Spec

Synthesize what's already been decided. Don't interview. If a decision the build needs is still open, list it under Open questions rather than picking for the user.

## 1. Ground it in the code

Read the parts of the repo the feature touches, plus its AGENTS.md, `docs/agents/`, and any design in `docs/architecture/` or `docs/decisions/`. Use the repo's own names for things. Find the existing pattern each new piece should copy, and name that file.

## 2. Pick the seams

Name where the feature will be tested, preferring seams that already exist and the highest one that's still fast. Confirm them with the user.

## 3. Write the file

Save to `docs/specs/<feature>.md`, or wherever the repo already keeps specs. Use this shape:

```markdown
# <Feature>

## Problem
What the user faces today, from their side.

## Behavior
Numbered, observable statements of what's true when this ships.
"A member who deletes their account can't sign back in."

## Decisions
Schema changes, module boundaries, interfaces, and anything settled in conversation.
Name the pattern file to copy. Inline a snippet only when it's the decision itself:
a type shape, a state machine, a schema.

## Tests
The agreed seams and what each one proves.

## Out of scope
What this deliberately leaves for later, so the builder doesn't add it.

## Open questions
Anything undecided. Empty is the goal.
```

Behavior lines are what `spec-review` checks against later, so each one must be checkable.

## 4. Write the brief

Below the spec, in the reply, write the prompt you'd paste into a fresh agent session. It points at the spec file instead of repeating it. It says what to build first, which skills to load (`tdd`, `verify`), the commands that must pass before it reports back, and that it ends with the commit-preparation summary from `git-workflow`.

name: tdd
description: Test-first development with red-green cycles. Use when asked to build or fix something test-first, write tests before code, do red-green-refactor, or add integration tests.
---

# TDD

Red, then green, one vertical slice at a time. Tests verify behavior through the public interface. Code inside can change completely and the tests shouldn't notice.

When this skill is active, it decides where tests go. That overrides ponytail's "one small test" default.

## Agree on the seams first

A **seam** is the public boundary you observe behavior through: a server function, a route, a module's exported API, a database query helper. Before writing any test, list the seams you plan to test, each with one line on what it catches and what it misses. Confirm them with the user. Prefer the highest seam that's still fast. One good seam beats five shallow ones.

Follow the repo's existing split between unit and integration tests. Read its testing doc first if it has one, like `docs/agents/testing.md`. Anything touching the database runs against a real test database, not a mocked client.

## The loop

1. Write one failing test for the next behavior at an agreed seam. Run it and watch it fail for the right reason.
2. Write only enough code to pass it.
3. Run the suite. Green.
4. Repeat with the next behavior. Each test is a tracer bullet that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

Writing all the tests first, then all the code, tests the shape you imagined rather than the behavior you built. Refactoring happens after the loop, during review.

## What makes a test worth keeping

- It calls the code the way a user or caller does and asserts the exact result they'd see, against a literal expected value.
- It survives a refactor that doesn't change behavior.
- Its name states a capability: "member can delete own comment", not "calls deleteComment".
- Mocks stand in only for what you can't run locally: third-party APIs, email, payment. The database, the router, and your own modules run for real.

Rewrite or delete a test that:

- would still pass if every imported function returned `undefined`
- recomputes the expected value the same way the code does, like `expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`
- verifies through a side channel, like querying the table directly instead of reading back through the interface
- breaks when you rename a private function

name: typescript
description: TypeScript conventions for writing, changing, or reviewing any .ts or .tsx file. Covers type safety at boundaries, modeling state with unions and branded types, and escape hatches to refuse.
---

# TypeScript

Make the compiler reject impossible states. When a type error appears, fix the mismatch it exposes. Project config, lint rules, and local AGENTS.md win over this file.

## Model the domain

- Model variants as a discriminated union with a literal discriminant. `{ kind: "open" } | { kind: "done"; at: Date }` beats `{ completed: boolean; completedAt?: Date }`. If you could write a comment explaining which field combinations are valid, it wants to be a union.
- Brand IDs and other semantic primitives so they can't be swapped: `type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: "UserId" }`. Create them once, at the boundary.
- Build the shape so the illegal value can't exist: `[T, ...T[]]` for non-empty, start plus duration for a range.
- Strengthen a type only where the loose one forces a `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. Otherwise keep the plain type.
- Derive types from the source that owns the shape: Drizzle tables (`$inferSelect`), Zod schemas (`z.infer`), `Parameters`, `ReturnType`, `Awaited`. Declare a parallel interface only when nothing owns it.
- Literal unions or `as const` arrays over `enum`.
- End every switch on a union with `const _exhaustive: never = value` so a new variant fails the build.

## Boundaries

External data is `unknown` until parsed: request bodies, JSON, env vars, `localStorage`, SDK responses, raw SQL results. Parse it once with the repo's schema library into a named domain type, then trust that type everywhere inside. Validation lives at the edge, business logic stays pure.

## Escape hatches

Each of these hides a real uncertainty. Establish the fact in code instead.

| Instead of | Write |
|---|---|
| `any` | `unknown`, then narrow |
| `value as User` | a parse function or a type guard that checks the claim |
| `value!` | an early return or a type that encodes presence |
| `as unknown as T` | a fix at the boundary where the type went wrong |
| `@ts-ignore` / `@ts-expect-error` in shipped code | the real type fix |

`satisfies` is the right tool for checking a shape while keeping literal types. Narrowing order: discriminant switch, then `in`, then `typeof`/`instanceof`, then a guard named `isX`. A cast survives only at a genuine boundary where the runtime fact is proven elsewhere, with a one-line comment naming that fact.

## Errors and async

- Catch as `unknown` and narrow before reading `.message`. Keep the original error as `cause` when wrapping.
- Every promise is awaited, returned, or explicitly `void`-ed with its failure handled.

## Readability

- Let inference handle locals. Annotate exported functions and module boundaries where the return type is the contract.
- Name units into values: `timeoutMs`, `priceCents`.
- Pass an options object when two arguments share a type or a boolean would switch modes.
- Generics must relate two types. A generic used once is a parameter.

name: unslop
description: Remove AI-writing tells from prose while keeping the author's meaning and voice. Use when writing or editing docs, READMEs, PR descriptions, commit messages, emails, messages, or any prose a person will read.
---

# Unslop

Write prose that sounds like a specific person with a point. Write it clean as you draft. A cleanup pass afterward misses most of these. Keep the author's meaning, tone, technical terms, humor, and formality. The goal is intentional writing, not bland writing.

## Punctuation and format

1. No em dashes or en dashes used as dashes. End the sentence or use a comma.
2. A colon goes before a list or an example, not as a connector in the middle of a sentence.
3. Fold parenthetical asides into the sentence or cut them. Don't swap dashes for parentheses.
4. Bold only what a reader needs to find. A bold label that restates its own line ("**Performance:** Performance improved") becomes plain prose.
5. Sentence-case headings, straight quotes, no decorative emoji.

## Words

6. Plain words: use, help, many, if, start, is, has. Not utilize, leverage, facilitate, numerous, in the event that, commence, serves as, stands as, boasts.
7. Watch the model's favorites when they're filler: additionally, crucial, delve, enhance, fostering, garner, intricate, landscape, pivotal, robust, seamless, showcase, tapestry, testament, underscore, vibrant.
8. Concrete nouns over technical-sounding metaphors: base not substrate, way not vector, add not wedge in, last phase not endgame. Keep jargon that is the actual technical term.
9. One name per thing. Don't rotate synonyms to avoid repetition.
10. Cut adverbs propping up weak verbs. "Runs quickly" becomes the number. "Significantly improves" becomes the measured change.
11. Delete filler: "it is important to note that", "in order to", "due to the fact that". Collapse stacked hedges to the real level of doubt.

## Sentences

12. Say what it does, not how it feels. "A column rename fails the build" beats "types that follow your schema". If a sentence could sit unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one.
13. Active voice with a named actor, unless the actor truly doesn't matter.
14. One idea per sentence when a sentence gets hard to parse. Vary length otherwise.
15. Write whole sentences. No arrows, dropped articles, or verbless fragments the reader has to decode.
16. Skip these shapes: "not just X, but Y", forced groups of three, "from X to Y" when X and Y aren't a range, trailing "-ing" phrases (highlighting, ensuring, reflecting), "despite challenges, X continues to thrive".
17. Name sources. "Experts believe" and "some argue" get a real source or get cut.

## Structure

18. Start with the useful information. No restating the prompt, no "here's why this matters" paragraph.
19. End on the decision, plan, or fact. No summary of what was just said, no "the future looks bright".
20. No chatbot lines: "Great question", "You're absolutely right", "I hope this helps", "Let me know if".
21. Let paragraphs be different shapes. Uniform symmetry reads generated.

## Final read

Read the result once without looking at the original and ask what still sounds generated. Fix that. Then check you didn't add opinions, certainty, or emotion the author didn't have.

name: verify
description: Prove a change works before calling it done, and find what it could break outside the diff. Use before reporting a task complete, when checking another agent's build summary against what it claims, or when asked what a change could break.
---

# Verify

"It compiles" and an agent's own summary are claims, not proof. Check the real artifact.

## 1. Restate the claim

Write down what the change is supposed to do, in observable terms: "a member who deletes their account can't log back in, and their posts still show as [deleted]." Pull it from the spec, the brief, or the agent's summary. When checking a summary, list each claim it makes as its own line.

## 2. Find the one fact it's safe because of

Most risky-looking changes are safe because of one fact, like "this query only ever runs inside the authed route group." Find it. If it holds, most risks clear at once. Then look where grep stops: the library's actual source at its pinned version, what runs at teardown or on retry, a DB column or JSON shape another app reads, a feature flag, code a few hops downstream.

## 3. Get each fact as far down this ladder as is cheap

1. Asserted. Worthless alone.
2. Pointed at a real `file:line` or the library's source.
3. Walked the failure case step by step and showed it can't happen.
4. Ran a script or test that calls the real code and fails loudly if you're wrong.
5. Reproduced it in the running app.

Rung 4 is usually one small script. Keep it so the user can rerun it instead of trusting you. When a check fails, suspect your check before the system. Read the actual value, not a cached or derived copy.

Done when every claim from step 1 has a rung, and the safety fact reaches rung 4 or 5 or is marked unproven.

## 4. Report

- **What it does.** Including the part the diff doesn't spell out.
- **Proven.** Each claim, its rung, and the command or output.
- **Unproven.** What you couldn't check and why.
- **Risks.** How it breaks, `file:line`, how likely, how bad, and the cheapest check.
- **Cleared.** What you checked that turned out fine.

Write it through `unslop`. Never hand the user a check you could have run yourself.

name: writing-for-agents
description: How to write documents agents read. Use when creating or editing a skill, an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, or any doc an agent reaches through a pointer, like docs/agents/.
---

# Writing for agents

A skill, an AGENTS.md, and a doc in `docs/agents/` are the same kind of thing: instructions an agent follows. The goal is that the agent takes the same process every run.

## Pointers decide when material loads

A skill's description and a line in AGENTS.md naming a doc are both **pointers**. The pointer's wording, not the target's content, decides whether the agent ever reads the target. When a skill doesn't fire, fix the pointer before touching the body.

- Lead with the word that triggers it. "Diagnosis loop for hard bugs" fires on bugs. "A structured methodology for..." fires on nothing.
- One trigger phrase per distinct case. Synonyms for one case are one case.
- Leave out anything the body already says.
- Every always-loaded line costs on every turn. AGENTS.md stays under about 50 lines, mostly pointers.

## Model-invoked or user-invoked

A skill with a model-facing description can fire on its own, and costs its description in every context. A skill with `disable-model-invocation: true` costs nothing until you type its name, but you have to remember it exists. Make it model-invoked only if the agent needs to reach it unprompted, or another skill points at it. Not every harness honors the flag, so give a user-invoked skill a short plain description that won't match ordinary requests.

Two skills whose descriptions match the same request make it a coin flip which one runs. Check new descriptions against existing ones, including plugin skills like ponytail's.

## Steps and reference

A document holds **steps** (what to do, in order) and **reference** (rules consulted as needed). Keep what every run needs in the main file. Move what only some runs need into a sibling file behind a pointer. Keep each concept's rule, example, and caveat together under one heading.

Every step ends on a **completion criterion** the agent can check: "every requirement and every hunk accounted for", not "review thoroughly". A vague criterion invites stopping early.

## Pruning

- **No-ops.** Delete any sentence the model already follows by default: "write clean code", "be careful", "follow best practices". The test is whether removing it changes behavior.
- **Caches.** Don't restate what one command or file shows: `package.json` scripts, directory layout, `--help`. Write down what looking won't reveal: unwritten conventions, the reason behind a choice, the gotcha.
- **Duplication.** Each rule lives in one place. Point to it from elsewhere.
- **Enforcement.** A rule that a lint, type, or test enforces needs at most one line naming what enforces it. Prefer building the check over writing the rule (see `correct`).
- **Staleness.** Point at one canonical example file instead of pasting large code blocks.

## Phrasing

- State the behavior you want. "Write one-line comments" works better than "don't write long comments", because a prohibition puts the unwanted behavior in front of the agent. Keep a prohibition only for a hard guardrail, and pair it with the positive version.
- Reuse a word the model already knows instead of defining a concept: *red* loop, *tracer bullet*, *seam*, *frontier*. A coined word costs its definition every time.
- Write it through `unslop`.

# dotfiles

My personal macOS dotfiles, managed with [GNU Stow](https://www.gnu.org/software/stow/).

## Quick Start

```shell
git clone git@github.com:loremipson/dotfiles.git ~/dotfiles
cd ~/dotfiles && ./install
```

The install script will:

1. Install [Homebrew](https://brew.sh) if not already present
2. Run `brew bundle` to install all dependencies from the `Brewfile`
3. Symlink all config packages into `$HOME` via Stow
4. Ask for your git name and email (saved to `~/.gitconfig`, not this repo)
5. Rebuild bat's theme cache
6. Install language runtimes with [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev)
7. Install [TPM](https://github.com/tmux-plugins/tpm) and the tmux plugins
8. Set zsh as the default shell if it isn't already

## Post-install

There's a couple things you'll want to do after (or before, honestly) installing.

- Set the Menu Bar in MacOS Settings to "Always" hide. You might want to enable the background as well, the default Menu Bar is still accessible by hovering at the top, and background enabled makes it easier to interact with.
- Change or remove the shortcut for MacOS Spotlight found in System Settings -> Keyboard -> Keyboard Shortcuts -> Spotlight. I set mine to `⌥+space` so that it's still accessible if I ever need it. Vicinae will operate with `⌘+space`.

## Re-running

The install script is safe to run again whenever. If a step fails, the rest still run, and you'll get a summary at the end with the command to rerun just that part.

```shell
./install                     # everything
./install mise tpm            # just these steps
./install stow git yazi       # just these packages (package names go after "stow")
./install --backup stow git   # move existing files out of the way, then stow
```

If Stow finds a real file where a symlink should go, it won't touch it. Run with `--backup` to move those files to `~/.dotfiles-backup/` first. Logs from every run end up in `~/.local/state/dotfiles/`.

## Git

Shared settings (delta, aliases, defaults) live in `~/.config/git/config`, which comes from this repo. Your name, email, and anything else personal go in `~/.gitconfig`, which stays yours. Git reads both, and `~/.gitconfig` wins if they overlap, so `git config --global` works like normal.

## Shell Commands

The Zsh config maps several familiar commands to newer tools:

| Command | Runs                            |
| ------- | ------------------------------- |
| `cat`   | `bat`                           |
| `ls`    | `eza` with Git status and icons |
| `tree`  | `eza --tree`                    |
| `cd`    | Zoxide's `z`                    |
| `grep`  | `rg`                            |
| `find`  | `fd`                            |

These tools do not support every option or behavior of the commands they replace. Add `_` to use the original command when needed: `cat_`, `ls_`, `grep_`, `find_`, or `cd_`.

## Language Versions

mise installs the default versions of Node, pnpm, Bun, Deno, and Go from `mise/.config/mise/config.toml`. To pin different versions for a project (or a whole folder of them), drop a `mise.toml` in that directory:

```toml
[tools]
node = "24"
pnpm = "11"
```

## Time Tracking (optional)

Tmux hooks can log session activity to [Timewarrior](https://timewarrior.net/) so time is tracked per tmux session. This is off by default, since it's only useful for specific situations, not every machine.

To enable it:

1. Create `~/.tmux.conf.local` with:

```tmux
   set-hook -g client-attached 'run-shell "~/.config/tmux/track-time.sh"'
   set-hook -g client-session-changed 'run-shell "~/.config/tmux/track-time.sh"'
   set-hook -g client-detached 'run-shell "~/.config/tmux/track-time.sh"'
```

2. Reload tmux config or restart the server.

Each tmux session name becomes a Timewarrior tag. View tracked time with `timew summary :all` or `timew day`.

## Workmux

This configuration uses [workmux](https://github.com/raine/workmux) to manage Git worktrees and their associated tmux sessions.

There are two supported workflows:

- **Git** — the default, for repositories using normal Git branches.
- **Graphite** — for repositories where Graphite owns the branch/stack topology and workmux owns the worktrees.

The workflow can be selected in `~/.tmux.conf.local`:

```tmux
set -g @workflow "graphite"
```

If no Graphite workflow is configured, the normal Git/workmux workflow is used.

Open the workmux menu with:

```text
prefix + w
```

Use the menu's `help` entry or run `man dotfiles-workmux` for the full Git and Graphite workflows.
